clue.text: Supplying charity, working closely together

parts.note: supplying something is handing it over
charity in the Biblical sense (faith, hope and charity) is love

explanation.surface: Someone describes giving to good causes as working together with others.
explanation.walkthrough: Charity is love in the Biblical sense (faith, hope and charity); the answer's real word breaks fall differently from the wordplay's.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes partners in close, often conspiratorial, cooperation, like a hand fitting its glove.

clue.text: Compared to maiden, men may be so alone

indicators.note: compared to sets the two words side by side so their difference shows

parts.note: taken as written: the letters left of maiden once the help in its middle goes
so points back at the comparison: men are the maiden lacking something, so this stands for less, without

explanation.surface: A puzzling remark comparing men with a maiden, about being alone.
explanation.walkthrough: An unusual reverse-style clue: set men beside maiden and the difference is AID, so men are the maiden 'without help'; 'so' stands for that state, which is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being without help means having nobody to assist you, so you are on your own.

clue.text: Trace source of beef in food outlet close to menagerie

parts.note: a deli (delicatessen) is a food shop
neat is an old word for cattle, the source of beef

indicators.note: close to means the end letter of menagerie

explanation.surface: Tracking down where the beef in a deli comes from, near a menagerie.
explanation.walkthrough: NEAT is an archaic word for cattle.
explanation.definitionFit: To delineate is to trace or outline the shape of something.

clue.text: Famous people: Newton and Watt, say, but not Jack

parts.note: N is the symbol for the newton, the unit of force

indicators.note: but not says the card's letter is dropped from the first name

parts.note: James Watt, the Scottish engineer, is one example of someone with that first name
J is the abbreviation for jack in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: Newton and Watt were famous people, but someone called Jack was not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newton and Watt' both look like units, but only Newton is; Watt gives his first name, JAMES.
explanation.definitionFit: Big names are celebrities, so names on their own can mean famous people.

clue.text: Girls this disappointed could change to become strong-willed

indicators.note: says the letters of girls with the answer rearrange to become the closing word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Disappointed girls might turn determined.
explanation.walkthrough: GIRLS plus the answer's letters rearranged ('could change to become') give STRONG-WILLED.
explanation.definitionFit: To be let down is to have one's hopes disappointed by someone.

clue.text: Article found in digs of Roman plain

indicators.note: found in says the article sits inside the house

parts.note: a villa was a Roman country house, digs being lodgings
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An object turned up in an archaeological dig of Roman remains on a plain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'digs' suggests excavation; it means lodgings, the Roman's villa.
explanation.definitionFit: Vanilla means plain or ordinary, from the most basic ice-cream flavour.

clue.text: Brainbox fixing business dispute in bank

indicators.note: fixing means fastening something into place
in says these pieces go inside the bank's letters

parts.note: BK is an abbreviation for bank
a right is a matter that is one's own concern, one's business
to spar is to argue, as in sparring partners

explanation.surface: A clever person settles a commercial disagreement at the bank.
explanation.walkthrough: RIGHT + SPAR go inside BK, an abbreviation for bank.
explanation.definitionFit: A bright spark is a clever, lively person, a brainbox.

clue.text: Disheartened slimmer sacked cheese deliverer, perhaps

indicators.note: sacked, as in plundered and ransacked, says the letters are thrown into a new order
disheartened says the central letter of slimmer is taken out

explanation.surface: A dieter, downcast, loses a job delivering cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cheese' is what you say for a photo: anyone who says it smiles.
explanation.definitionFit: People say cheese to a camera to make themselves grin, so someone delivering that word is grinning.

clue.text: Ring for projector to screen government department reform

indicators.note: to screen something is to hide it behind or within, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: a reel is the wound ring of film fed through a projector
MOD is the Ministry of Defence, a UK government department

explanation.surface: A cinema projectionist's ring of film shown to a ministry about to be reformed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' tempts as O; the whole phrase 'Ring for projector' is the film reel. MOD is Britain's Ministry of Defence.
explanation.definitionFit: To reform something is to reshape or restructure it, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Insurgency you reported within two minutes

indicators.note: within says one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: minute in two senses: M is the abbreviation for a minute of time, and minute (my-NEWT) means tiny

indicators.note: reported means heard rather than written, so the word is replaced by a letter of the same sound

parts.note: the word you said aloud is the letter U

explanation.surface: A rebellion seems to be announced with only two minutes' warning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'two minutes' gives two different senses of the word: M (a minute of time) and TINY (minute meaning very small), with U placed between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A mutiny is an uprising against authority, a kind of insurgency.

clue.text: Dry area torched, that is start of several cruel deeds

parts.note: brut describes very dry champagne
torched means set alight, lit
ie is the abbreviation of id est, that is

indicators.note: start of takes the opening letter of several

explanation.surface: A dry region burnt, the start of a series of savage acts.
explanation.definitionFit: Brutalities are savage acts of violence, synonymous with cruel deeds.

clue.text: Craft and impudence required to confront energy provider

indicators.note: to confront is to stand in front of, so the first piece comes before the second

parts.note: gall is cheek or impudence
E.ON is a UK energy supply company

explanation.surface: It takes cunning and cheek to take on the energy company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craft' looks like cunning, paired with impudence, but it is the definition: a ship. E.ON supplies gas and electricity in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A galleon is a large sailing ship, and craft is a general word for vessels.

clue.text: Giveaway section on flier

definitions.meaning: something that reveals a plot or result in advance
a hinged flap on an aircraft wing that reduces lift

explanation.surface: A free gift is part of a printed leaflet.
explanation.definitionFit: A spoiler both reveals a plot ahead of time and is a lift-dumping panel on a plane's wing.

clue.text: Figure to trust endlessly

indicators.note: endlessly says the word trust loses its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A number one can rely on without limit.
explanation.definitionFit: A torus is a geometric figure, the ring-doughnut shape.

clue.text: Rising when American's ready, embracing and moving

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

indicators.note: embracing says the coin holds the next piece inside it

parts.note: ready is cash, and a cent is a piece of American money

indicators.note: moving says the letters of the word and are shifted into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone rises when the American is ready, hugging and moving.
explanation.walkthrough: Ready is British slang for cash; 'moving' makes DAN, which 'embracing' holds inside the coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascendant describes something on the way up, as a star or a career, so it fits rising.

clue.text: Pound invested in long-term European account

indicators.note: invested in says the pound is placed inside the other letters

parts.note: chronic describes an illness that lasts a long time
L is the abbreviation for pound, from libra

explanation.surface: Money put into a long-term European bank account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'invested', 'pound' and 'account' all point to banking; account is the definition, a record of events.
explanation.definitionFit: A chronicle is a historical account of events in order.

clue.text: Soldiers returned attack, cutting noble fellow after a killing

indicators.note: cutting says the pieces slice into the noble's letters

parts.note: a peer is a member of the nobility

indicators.note: returned says the soldiers' letters are read back to front

parts.note: OR is short for other ranks, ordinary soldiers
a fit is a sudden attack, as of coughing

explanation.surface: Troops strike back, slicing into an aristocrat after a murder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a killing' is a sudden huge profit, not a murder.
explanation.definitionFit: A profiteer is someone out to make excessive gains, idiomatically looking to make a killing.

clue.text: Dictionary one friend finds kind of complex

parts.note: OED is the Oxford English Dictionary
I is the Roman numeral one
a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: Someone with a dictionary and a friend discovers a type of complex.
explanation.definitionFit: Freud's Oedipus complex is the best-known psychological complex, so the adjective names one kind.

clue.text: First person on death row ain't, oddly, American

parts.note: I is the first person singular pronoun

indicators.note: oddly takes the first, third, fifth letters and so on of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A first-person claim that a man on death row is not American.
explanation.walkthrough: The odd letters of DEATH ROW AIN'T are D, A, H, O, A, N.
explanation.definitionFit: An Idahoan comes from the US state of Idaho, and so is an American.

clue.text: Veg and game that's encased in shellfish

parts.note: a pea is a vegetable
RL is rugby league

explanation.surface: A dinner of vegetables and game meat served inside seafood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game' sounds like venison but is rugby league.
explanation.definitionFit: A pearl forms inside an oyster or other mollusc, so it is the thing an oyster's shell holds.

clue.text: Acted upon free ticket given without restriction

parts.note: a pass is a ticket letting you in free

indicators.note: without restriction says the word given loses its outer letters, its limits

explanation.surface: Someone did something with a complimentary ticket handed over freely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without restriction' looks like 'freely' but strips the ends off GIVEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Passive describes a subject that is acted on rather than acting, as in grammar.

clue.text: Odour rising with liberal being without ethics

indicators.note: rising in a down entry says the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: an aroma is a smell or odour

explanation.surface: A smell goes up alongside a liberal with no morals.
explanation.definitionFit: Amoral means having no moral principles at all, so lacking ethics.

clue.text: Issue developing from head waiter ignoring that man and wife or a maitre d' ignoring male

indicators.note: developing says the remaining letters change into a new form
ignoring says these letters are left out of the head waiter's letters

parts.note: he is a pronoun for that man

explanation.surface: Something emerges from a head waiter, or from a maitre d' who ignores a man.
explanation.walkthrough: Two parallel recipes: 'ignoring' takes HE and W from HEADWAITER, leaving ADAITER; or 'ignoring male' takes M from A MAITRE D, leaving AAITRED. Either set rearranged ('developing') gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To radiate is to issue or emit outward, as light from a source.

clue.text: Odd text rankled somewhat

indicators.note: somewhat says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Strangely, a message annoyed someone a little.
explanation.definitionFit: Odd can mean spare or additional, as in odd socks left over, so it fits surplus.

clue.text: Slowly get into the flow, not covering most of Asian capital

indicators.note: covering says the first word wraps round the other piece

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: most of says the capital loses its last letter

parts.note: Seoul is the capital of South Korea

explanation.surface: Easing into a stream while avoiding most of an Asian city.
explanation.walkthrough: The flow is traffic: a driver edges out into it.
explanation.definitionFit: To nose out is to edge a vehicle carefully forward into moving traffic.

clue.text: Forcibly remove guard for nothing in middle of duty

indicators.note: guard says the outer letters stand round the pieces they protect
middle of takes the central letters of the word duty

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A guard is forcibly removed for doing nothing while on duty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'guard' looks like a noun but is the verb: the middle letters of 'duty' stand round the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To uproot is to tear out by the roots, so to remove by force.

clue.text: Moneymaking invention

definitions.meaning: the creation of a new word or phrase

explanation.definitionFit: Coinage is both the making of coins and the inventing of new words.

clue.text: Mole with information given during meal about royal dynasty

parts.note: a plant is a spy placed inside an organisation, like a mole

indicators.note: given during says the information goes inside the meal's letters
about says the meal's letters are turned round

parts.note: tea is a meal
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: A spy gets secrets over dinner about the royal family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns the meal round to AET; 'given during' then puts the information inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Plantagenets were the English ruling house from Henry II to Richard III.
